Anxiety

/ang-ZY-uh-tee/ - the stress falls on ZY · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Anxiety means intense worry and uneasiness.

In the week before her road test, a low hum of anxiety followed Priya everywhere, even into her dreams.

Worked Example

As the forecast hardened into a hail warning, anxiety settled over the orchard house. Nobody said much at dinner; Mara kept walking to the window to check a sky that had not changed, while her father re-read the crop insurance papers he already knew by heart.

Anxiety is stronger than worry or concern: it names worry grown intense enough to occupy the body and refuse to be set down - the pacing, the rechecking, the appetite that disappears. Concern thinks about a problem now and then; anxiety cannot stop.

How Anxiety Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

worry

worry: everyday troubled thoughts, milder and easier to set aside

unease

unease: a vague sense that something is off, less intense

apprehension

apprehension: worry pointed at one specific coming event

Antonyms

calm

calm: a settled, untroubled state of mind

assurance

assurance: confident freedom from doubt

How Strong Is It? — concern → worry → anxiety → panic

concern vs. anxiety

concern vs. anxiety: Concern notices a problem and thinks it over; it stays in the mind's front office and clocks out at night, while anxiety follows you home.

worry vs. anxiety

worry vs. anxiety: Worry chews on a problem off and on; anxiety grips harder - it is worry grown intense enough to show up in your body.

panic vs. anxiety

panic vs. anxiety: Panic goes past anxiety entirely: anxiety is intense unease you still function through, while panic floods in and overwhelms you in the moment.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of anxiety.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — anxi-

Root — anxi-: to choke, to squeeze (Latin angere)

Suffix — -ety

Suffix — -ety: state of being (a variant of -ity)

Put it together

Put it together: Anxi- (from Latin angere, 'to choke, to squeeze') + -ety (the state of being; a spelling variant of -ity) = the state of being squeezed. The Romans located the feeling in the body - a tightness of chest and throat - and English keeps the adjective anxious, so anxiety is literally the state of being anxious. Notice the spelling: after certain stems the suffix surfaces as -ety rather than -ity.

Use the root in a new word: angina

Use the root in a new word: angina: Doctors call the chest-squeezing pain of a strained heart angina - the same Latin choke-and-squeeze root, naming a pressure you can physically feel.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Anxiety is the standard word, equally at home in conversation and in clinical writing. Choose worry for lighter, passing trouble; choose anxiety when the distress is intense, lasting, or physical. The adjective anxious describes the person; anxiety names the state itself.
